issues.description: The manuscript gives mutually incompatible descriptions of the sample. The abstract, introduction, discussion, and conclusion describe a national probability/general-population/nationally representative sample, whereas the Methods describe a small introductory psychology participant-pool sample. These designs imply different target populations, recruitment mechanisms, weighting needs, attrition patterns, and generalizability. This contradiction undermines the interpretation of the entire study.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years. We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The manuscript claims high generalizability to New Zealand despite reporting a young, mostly female, mostly Pākehā introductory psychology sample. If the Methods are accurate, the sample is a convenience student sample, not representative of the New Zealand population. Even if the NZAVS claim is intended, no weighting or representativeness diagnostics are reported.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population. Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).

issues.description: The reported Time 1 correlations, p values, and confidence intervals are not plausible for the stated N = 374. For example, r = -.08 with n = 374 would yield approximately p = .12, not p < .001. The confidence intervals are also far too narrow for n = 374; r = .21 would have a 95% CI of roughly .11 to .30, not .18 to .23. The mean CIs are similarly too narrow. This indicates either an incorrect sample size, incorrect inferential statistics, or copied results from a different dataset.

The reported RMSEA is mathematically incompatible with the stated N = 374, chi-square = 36511.73, and df = 2279. Using the standard RMSEA formula, these values imply an RMSEA of approximately .20, not .03. The reported fit indices therefore cannot all be correct simultaneously.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The study uses five waves of longitudinal data but provides no wave-by-wave retention, dropout rates, missingness patterns, or comparison of retained versus lost participants. Listwise deletion assumes complete-case data are representative under restrictive missingness conditions; in a five-wave study this can introduce serious attrition bias and reduce power. Referring readers to an external website is insufficient for evaluating the manuscript.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website. Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2, but the manuscript does not explain how this planned missingness was handled in scale construction or modeling. This is especially problematic because the analysis used listwise deletion; if item-level models were used, listwise deletion would remove all participants with the missing Time 2 item unless special handling was implemented. If composites were used, the Time 2 RWA score is based on a different item set than the other waves.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points. Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the outcome as willingness to change behavior or willingness to sacrifice, but the Methods define environmentalism as concern about environmental problems using two attitudinal/skepticism items. Environmental concern, perceived exaggeration, behavioral willingness, and actual behavior are distinct constructs. This mismatch threatens construct validity and makes the substantive interpretation of the cross-lagged paths unclear.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”. We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.description: The theoretical framing and discussion repeatedly concern climate change denial, climate change mitigation, and climate communications, but the measured outcome is a broad two-item environmental concern/exaggeration measure. General environmental concern cannot be assumed to measure climate-change denial, climate-change action, or mitigation willingness. This creates a construct-to-claim mismatch.
issues.quote: Keywords: Social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, environmentalism, climate change. Research on the psychological foundations of climate change denial have highlighted the important role of two ideological attitudes... Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications.

issues.description: Several items are reverse-keyed relative to the constructs, including SDO equality items and the environmental-problems-exaggerated item. The manuscript does not state which items were reverse-coded, how scale scores were computed, whether items were averaged or modeled as indicators, or whether higher scores consistently indicate greater SDO/RWA/environmentalism. This prevents replication and makes interpretation of coefficients uncertain.
issues.quote: Three items favoured dominance, such as “To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups”, and three favoured equality, such as “We should have increased social equality”. Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems... “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: Longitudinal cross-lagged interpretation requires that constructs are measured equivalently across time. The manuscript reports neither configural, metric, scalar, nor residual invariance tests. This omission is particularly serious because the RWA item set changes at Time 2. Apparent change or cross-lagged effects may reflect changing measurement properties rather than changes in the latent constructs.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points. We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The analysis is described as path analysis among three variables, which suggests observed scale scores, but the authors also discuss constraining item residual variances over time, which implies an item-level latent variable SEM. The manuscript does not specify the measurement model, factor loadings, item intercepts, residual covariances, latent scaling, or whether composites or latent factors were used. This ambiguity makes the analysis non-replicable.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment. The model included three variables across five measurement points... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The Methods state that standardized parameters are presented, but the Figure caption and Results report unstandardized coefficients. Standardized and unstandardized parameters answer different questions and affect whether cross-path comparisons are meaningful. This inconsistency obscures interpretation.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The Data Analysis section repeats the same constraint on cross-lagged paths and does not clearly state whether autoregressive paths, factor loadings, intercepts, contemporaneous covariances, residual covariances, or means were constrained. This is a major omission for a stationary longitudinal SEM.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points. Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The authors impose time-invariant cross-lagged effects because of their substantive interest, but do not report tests comparing constrained and unconstrained models or examine whether effects plausibly differ across waves. If developmental, historical, or measurement changes occurred from 2009 to 2013, stationarity constraints could bias estimates and conceal meaningful heterogeneity.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The manuscript describes a five-year study, five time points, and five semesters from 2009 to 2013. Five semesters is not five years, and 2009 to 2013 could imply four years elapsed depending on dates. The exact spacing of waves is not reported, yet cross-lagged coefficients depend on the time interval between measurements.
issues.quote: Full title: The influence of social dominance orientation and right-wing authoritarianism on environmentalism: A five-year cross-lagged analysis. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The model is accepted despite very poor chi-square and CFI. A CFI of .86 is generally below accepted thresholds for adequate fit, and the very large chi-square indicates substantial misfit. The authors dismiss these indices as affected by complexity but accept the model based on RMSEA and SRMR alone, without considering misspecification, residual diagnostics, or alternative models.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The authors test whether the SDO-to-environmentalism and RWA-to-environmentalism paths differ by constraining them equal. The comparison is non-significant, p = .126, meaning the data do not provide evidence that the paths differ. The authors nevertheless interpret SDO as the stronger predictor based on coefficient pattern, and the Discussion later states SDO is significantly stronger. This is an inferential error.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample. In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.

issues.description: The reported RWA cross-lagged effect has internally inconsistent inferential statistics. If SD is intended as the standard error, B = -.02 with SE = .01 would not typically yield p = .001, and the 95% CI width is also inconsistent with p = .001. If SD is not a standard error, the basis for the p value and CI is unclear.
issues.quote: Indeed, SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The manuscript reports path estimates as B followed by SD, p, and CI. Inferential statistics for regression/path coefficients are normally reported with standard errors, not standard deviations. If these are standard errors, the label is wrong; if they are standard deviations, the inferential statistics are insufficiently specified.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: Several model-comparison statistics are written as '2(1)' rather than χ²(1), and at least one value is implausibly enormous relative to the reported coefficients. For example, χ²(1) = 15,389.13 for comparing two very small paths suggests either a typographical error, a scaling problem, or a faulty model comparison. Misreported test statistics prevent evaluation of the conclusions.

The authors compare the magnitudes of reciprocal paths across different outcomes using unstandardized coefficients. Unstandardized coefficients depend on the scaling and variance of both predictor and outcome; in latent models they can also depend on arbitrary factor scaling. Claims that one direction is 'stronger' than the reverse require standardized effects, comparable scaling, or a clearly justified model constraint.
issues.quote: However, while the association between SDO and environmentalism was bidirectional, the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse (2(1) = 39.97, p < .001), whilst there was no difference between the strength of the effect of RWA on environmentalism and vice versa (2(1) = 2.70, p = .100).

issues.description: The manuscript makes strong causal claims from observational survey data. Cross-lagged associations do not establish causality because of unmeasured confounding, measurement error, stable between-person differences, and possible omitted time-varying variables. The data can support temporal prediction, not claims that ideology causes environmentalism or that desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment. With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes. This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future

issues.description: The manuscript interprets cross-lagged paths as changes within individuals, but a traditional cross-lagged panel model can conflate stable between-person differences with within-person processes. Without a random-intercept CLPM, latent change model, or other decomposition, the analysis cannot determine whether people who are higher than others in SDO subsequently change in environmentalism, versus stable trait-like differences producing the association.
issues.quote: The findings from our cross-lagged paths provide support for past research that has indicated SDO to be an important predictor of environment-related attitudes... These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships, and suggest that SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse.

issues.description: The model includes only SDO, RWA, and environmentalism. No demographic, political, socioeconomic, personality, cohort, or period covariates are included, despite plausible confounding of ideology-environment associations. The authors acknowledge possible third-variable explanations only after making causal interpretations.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points... Given the bidirectionality of our findings, a possible alternative explanation is that the relationship between ideology and environmentalism across time is explained by a third variable.

issues.description: If the study is truly based on a national probability or nationally representative sample, analyses should report whether sampling weights, post-stratification weights, clustering, and design effects were used. None are described. If weights were not used, estimates may not be population-representative; if the sample was instead a participant pool, the representativeness claim is false.
issues.quote: We examine the longitudinal influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment in a national probability sample over five years. We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report preregistration, an a priori analysis plan, or criteria for model specification, constraints, inclusion/exclusion, or alternative models. The authors describe choosing constraints based on interests and make post hoc interpretive decisions after a non-significant difference test. This creates researcher degrees of freedom that could affect conclusions.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured. A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The analysis syntax is promised only after acceptance, which prevents reviewers from verifying model constraints, missing-data handling, estimator choice, and parameter comparisons. For a complex longitudinal SEM with internal inconsistencies, this omission materially limits reproducibility and peer review.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The Methods provide almost no information about recruitment procedures, survey administration, compensation, consent, inclusion/exclusion criteria, wave timing, or retention. Directing readers to a website does not provide sufficient information within the manuscript to evaluate or replicate the study.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The measures use 7-point Likert-type responses, but the manuscript does not report the Mplus estimator, whether items were treated as continuous or ordinal, whether robust standard errors were used, or how non-normality was handled. These choices can affect fit indices, standard errors, and cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales, from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptives, correlations, and reliabilities are reported. A five-wave longitudinal analysis requires wave-specific means, variances, reliabilities, missingness, and correlations to evaluate stability, change, stationarity, attrition, and measurement quality across time.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1. Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: The Results state that all constructs were relatively stable over time but do not provide the autoregressive coefficients, confidence intervals, or exact tests in the text. If the figure is unavailable or incomplete, readers cannot evaluate the magnitude of stability or compare it across constructs.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time, consistent with our prediction that these variables remain largely unchanged over the study period.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states that p < .05 is the accepted threshold, whereas the Figure caption says all paths meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. The manuscript does not explain why different thresholds are used, which paths are evaluated at which threshold, or whether any adjustment for multiple comparisons was considered.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL). All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The authors justify their significance threshold by referring to a large sample, but the Methods report only 374 participants. N = 374 is not a large sample for a complex five-wave item-level SEM with many parameters and small cross-lagged effects. This again suggests a mismatch between the described sample and the analyzed data.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: The table note says confidence intervals are based on 1000 iterations but does not identify the procedure, such as nonparametric bootstrap, Monte Carlo simulation, or another method. The CI method, resampling unit, and handling of missing data are necessary for reproducibility, especially because the intervals appear inconsistent with the stated N.
issues.quote: Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.description: If the reported N = 374 is correct, the model is highly complex relative to the sample size, with 2279 degrees of freedom and many repeated indicators/paths. The manuscript reports no power analysis, sensitivity analysis, or simulation showing adequate power for small cross-lagged effects such as B = -.02. This is particularly concerning given listwise deletion and attrition.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001... RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The manuscript infers that the observed associations reflect motivation to exploit the environment, desire for dominance, and desire to submit to authority. None of these mechanisms were directly measured in relation to environmental attitudes, and the outcome is not environmental exploitation. The causal-motivational interpretation goes beyond the data.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to authority.

issues.description: The manuscript discusses RWA dimensions and concludes that effects reflect submission to authority and tradition, but the analysis uses a short composite RWA scale and does not model authoritarian submission, aggression, and conventionalism separately. Given prior evidence cited by the authors that RWA dimensions can have different associations with environmentalism, the composite cannot support dimension-specific conclusions.
issues.quote: However, Reese [20] found that the dimensions of RWA differentially predict pro-environmental attitudes: authoritarian submission predicts greater pro-environmentalism, authoritarian aggression predicts lower pro-environmentalism, whilst the preference for tradition is unrelated. This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future, which is influenced to a lesser extent by the desire to submit to authority and tradition.

issues.description: The discussion reframes environmentalism as a hierarchy-attenuating ideology and uses this to interpret SDO effects. The study did not measure hierarchy attenuation, perceived distribution of environmental harms/benefits, environmental justice attitudes, or support for policies benefiting subordinate groups. This theoretical interpretation is plausible but not tested by the data.
issues.quote: Gaining similar opposition from Social Dominants, environmentalism is a hierarchy-attenuating ideology: Exploitation of natural resources favours the dominant group, while the consequences fall to those at the bottom of the hierarchy.

issues.description: The manuscript interprets a lagged path from RWA to SDO as evidence that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. Socialization processes were not measured, and the observational cross-lagged association cannot identify socialization mechanisms or national-level ideological development.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses behavioral language, including willingness to change behavior and behave pro-environmentally, but the reported items assess concern and perceived exaggeration rather than behavior or behavioral intention. This risks overstating implications for actual environmental action.
issues.quote: Our study specifically examines the influence of SDO and RWA on people’s willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment in a New Zealand general population sample. Specifically, from our results we cannot pinpoint the rationale behind why those high in SDO are less willing to behave pro-environmentally.

issues.description: The Discussion contrasts the present study with prior student-sample work by saying the present study used a general population sample. This is inconsistent with the Methods statement that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool.
issues.quote: This pattern of results, where SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA, is the reverse of the pattern obtained from the first longitudinal analysis on this topic, which showed that RWA was the stronger predictor among students [14]. However, this difference in findings is consistent with expectations based on the results of Stanley and Wilson’s [22] meta-analysis, which showed that the association with SDO is significantly weaker in student samples. It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.
